title: Act III, Scene III

teacherSummary.text: At dusk a mysterious Third Murderer joins the first two. Banquo and Fleance approach on foot from the palace gate with a torch. The murderers attack and kill Banquo, who cries to Fleance to fly and avenge him. The light is struck out and Fleance escapes. The murderers go to report how much is done.

segments.script: The identity of the Third Murderer is never explained; some productions make him Macbeth himself, Ross or Seyton, showing Macbeth's distrust even of his hired men. Fleance's escape keeps the Witches' prophecy for Banquo's line alive and marks the first time Macbeth's plans fail. Plot: Three murderers (a third appears unexplained) kill Banquo; Fleance escapes. Imagery: Dusk, a torch put out. Irony: The prophecy about Banquo's heirs survives in Fleance. Watch for darkness and light: Night and darkness hide crimes; the Macbeths call on darkness to cover their deeds, and putting out a light marks murder.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “The west yet glimmers with some streaks of day” slowly and put it in my own words: The First Murderer says the west still glimmers with streaks of day. Next, craft. I notice the gentle, poetic description from a hired killer. The strongest word is “glimmers”: it shows the last light before darkness, as Banquo's life is about to end. Then, effect. Why does the murderer describe the fading light? My answer: The fading light marks Banquo's death; the beauty of the line contrasts with the violence to come.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the scene for plot, imagery (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about Banquo's murder and Fleance's escape? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Act III, Scene III develops the idea of Banquo's murder and Fleance's escape. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of setting and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Fleance's escape shows that Macbeth cannot control the future the witches foretold. When the text says “O, treachery! Fly, good Fleance, fly, fly, fly” (Act III, Scene III, line 1187), it shows this directly. Banquo's dying cry "Fly, good Fleance, fly" saves his son, and the murderers admit they "have lost / Best half of our affair."

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
